passage: On the morning of Sankranti, Sharmila was up before the cows, drawing rangoli at the door of the old house in the village. Her mother-in-law Minakshi watched from the verandah, approving the fine white lines. Sharmila touched her feet, served the sesame sweets to Minakshi first, and sat through the whole puja. Later, on the verandah, Minakshi said the couple should give up the town flat and move back home. Sharmila glanced at her husband Ravi. It was Ravi who spoke. "Maa, we've decided to stay in town for now. Sharmila's job is there, and we'll come for every festival." Minakshi's mouth thinned. Sharmila poured her tea and said only, "We'll be here for Holi too, Maa-ji."

qa.q: What did Sharmila draw at the door of the old house?
qa.a: She drew rangoli, fine white lines, at the door.

qa.q: What might Minakshi be feeling after Ravi's answer, and what suggests it?
qa.a: She may feel disappointed and worried about losing them from the house, as her thinned mouth suggests, though it is only a cue and not proof.

qa.q: Why did it help that Ravi, not Sharmila, told Minakshi about staying in town?
qa.a: The limit came from her own son, so it did not look like a daughter-in-law turning him away, while Sharmila kept showing respect through rituals and tea.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt when Ravi answered his mother?
qa.a: Sharmila was probably relieved that Ravi spoke for them, since she had glanced at him, and she stayed respectful by pouring tea and promising to come for Holi.

grounding: Shows a daughter-in-law honouring rituals and courtesy while the couple's decision is stated first by the husband.

Every Lunar New Year, Gabriel flew with Jin to her parents' house outside Busan. He had learned to bow properly, to pour for her father with two hands, and to eat the rice-cake soup that meant another year of life.

This year her parents raised it at dinner: when the baby came, they expected the couple to move into the family house.

Gabriel felt his throat tighten. He had promised himself not to argue at their table.

Jin put down her spoon first. "Appa, Umma, thank you for wanting us close. We've decided to stay in Seoul. We'll visit every month, and you'll have a room with us whenever you like."

Her mother looked at Gabriel. He bowed his head slightly. "We want the baby to know you well. Jin and I decided together."

Her father was quiet, then refilled Gabriel's glass. It wasn't agreement, but it wasn't a fight.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling when the parents raised the move?
qa.a: Gabriel felt tense and anxious, with a tight throat, wanting to stay respectful and avoid arguing at their table.

qa.q: Why was it wise that Jin spoke first?
qa.a: Jin, as their daughter, could state the couple's limit to her own parents kindly, while Gabriel showed respect and backed the decision.

qa.q: How might Jin's father see the refilled glass moment?
qa.a: It may show he feels disappointed but still accepts Gabriel with respect, choosing warmth over a fight.

grounding: Shows a son-in-law honouring his in-laws' rituals while the couple protects its decision, with his wife speaking first to her parents.

The community hall in Indore was booked for the baby's naming ceremony, and Sarika's in-laws had arrived with a list: two hundred guests, a priest from their village and a name chosen by the family astrologer.

Sarika and Chetan had already chosen the name Aarohi, and they wanted forty guests.

Before Sarika could say anything, Chetan took his parents into the side room. Through the door she heard him speak calmly. "Maa, Papa, we'd love the priest to do the puja, and we'll follow every ritual you want. But the name is Aarohi, and we're keeping it small. This is our decision together."

When they came out, Chetan's mother looked hurt. Sarika went to her, touched her feet and said, "Maa, will you tie the thread on Aarohi's wrist? It would mean a lot to us."

Her mother-in-law hesitated, then nodded. At the ceremony, she was the one who whispered the name into the baby's ear first.

qa.q: How many guests did Sarika and Chetan want?
qa.a: Sarika and Chetan wanted forty guests.

qa.q: What was Chetan's mother feeling when she came out of the side room?
qa.a: Chetan's mother felt hurt and disappointed that her plans for the name and guests had been refused.

qa.q: What did Sarika and Chetan do well in handling the in-laws?
qa.a: Chetan spoke to his own parents first and calmly, and Sarika showed respect through a ritual invitation, keeping their decisions while honouring the family.

qa.q: How might the ceremony have felt different for Sarika if she had argued with her in-laws herself?
qa.a: Sarika might have been seen as the one defying the family, making the tension personal and harder to heal.

grounding: Shows a couple honouring in-laws through courtesy and ritual while protecting their own decisions, with the husband speaking to his parents first.
